newsitem.title: UK: Smith & Nephew skin graft on target.
newsitem.headline: Smith & Nephew skin graft on target.

text.p: British healthcare group Smith & Nephew Plc said on Tuesday it was on target to launch a revolutionary new skin graft treatment later this year, although analysts are divided over its potential.

The company and its U.S. partner Advanced Tissue Sciences Inc said results from a 12-week and 32-week trial of the new product, Dermagraft, in diabetics with serious foot ulcers were "statistically significant".

Dermagraft allows living cells derived from babies' foreskins, a readily available source whose cells are more active than normal skin, to grow on a naturally-absorbable scaffold across wounds. The companies said that a trial of 235 chronic diabetics showed that 60 percent more patients saw their wounds heal completely than those given current standard treatments.
However, the announcement had only a marginal impact on the group's shares, which were up 2 3/4 pence at 181 1/4 in early afternoon trading, reflecting investors' uncertainty.

The stock remains well below the peaks of around 217 pence achieved last June, after the joint venture with Advanced Tissue Sciences was announced, and in October, when optimism about Dermagraft was high.

Analysts said Smith & Nephew had to regain ground after disappointment over a previous trial result last autumn led to broker downgrades and sent its shares sharply lower, touching a low of 171 pence in February this year.
The stock has moved from outperforming the FT-SE All Share index by nearly 11 percent last October to an underperformance of nine percent currently, according to Reuters 3000 data.

Peter Cartwright of Williams de Broe said the results of the latest trial, presented to a medical conference in New Orleans, were "significant but probably not pivotal." Cartwright said the trial results were "fairly, if expected, good news. If the results had been bad it would have been a different story."

But Panmure Gordon analyst Robin Gilbert said Tuesday's announcement was a milestone. He believes a $1 billion market could develop for products like Dermagraft, with Smith & Nephew enjoying the advantage of being first on the scene.
"I think this could be a very significant product. Because it is in a rather unfamiliar area people are ignoring its potential," Gilbert said.

And he added that Dermagraft "could be the Zantac of the healthcare sector," noting the slow start to the Glaxo Wellcome Plc anti-ulcerant which eventually became the world's best-selling drug for 11 successive years.

Foot ulcers are a major problem for chronic diabetics, who often lose sensation in the foot and leg and are unaware of damage built up by pressure on the lower limbs. The complication, which can result in amputation, is costly to treat, making a product like Dermagraft economically attractive.

However, Dermagraft faces a number of potential competing products, including Apligraf, which is being developed by Organogenesis Inc and Novartis AG, and Regranex, under development by Chiron Corp and Johnson and Johnson.
Apligraf, seen as the most serious rival, was approved for use in venous ulcers in Canada last week.

Analysts said competition could make it harder to sustain premium prices for Dermagraft. However, the product is seen as a major shift for Smith & Nephew into high-tech, high margin products, and the group is also investing heavily in cartilage replacement and bone substitute products.

In a recent note, analysts at Salomon Brothers predicted revenues from Dermagraft of 102 million pounds ($165.3 million) in 1998, and peak sales of 300 million pounds in 2003. They said the product could be worth 30 pence per share in the Smith & Nephew price.
